lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- Checkpoint 1: Ten Minutes About Me
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Giovanna de Fátima | Lesson 10 -- Checkpoint 1: Ten Minutes About Me

listenings.text: Hi Giovanna, Greg here. You asked me what people ask a new engineer in the first ten minutes. I made a list on the plane, and it is always the same five. One: what is your background? Two: what exactly do you do here, on a normal day? Three: how long is your commute? Everybody asks that one, and nobody knows why. Four: what are you working on at the moment? And five, usually at the end, when the coffee arrives: what do you do at the weekend? That is it. Five questions, and the answer to each one is about four sentences. Nobody wants a lecture. I prepared my five answers before my first day here, and I still use them. Prepare yours. Ten minutes is not a long time when you know what is coming.

Hi Giovanna, it is Karen. One thing about your ten minutes, because I think about this a lot. Everybody loses a word. I lose words in my own language, in meetings, every week. The problem is not the word: the problem is the silence after it, when you stop and start again in Portuguese. So learn three small sentences and use them. The first one: sorry, could you say that again? The second one: I do not know the word in English, but it is the thing we use to move the earth. The third one, and this is my favorite: let me start again. People wait. Nobody is timing you and nobody cares about the word. They care that you keep going. In my first year here I said sorry, could you say that again about four hundred times, and here I am.

extra_audio.text: First she says her name, her age and what she does. Then she talks about her background and her degree. After that she describes a normal day, from the alarm to the end of the shift. Then she describes the site, and where everything is. Then she says what she can do and what she cannot do yet. Finally she talks about last weekend and about what she likes.

paras: My name is Karen Booth and I am a tunnel engineer in London. I am thirty-four. When I meet somebody new on a site, the first ten minutes are always the same five questions, so one evening I sat down and wrote my answers. Here they are.

My background is not the one people expect. I have a degree in geology, not in engineering. I studied for four years, I worked in a laboratory for three more, and then I changed. I started in this company in 2019, in the east of London, and I never went back to the laboratory.

My day always starts at six. First I make coffee, then I take the train, and after that I walk twenty minutes from the station to the gate. My commute takes fifty minutes each way, and I read on the train, every day. I usually get home at seven. When there is a problem underground I do overtime, and then I get home at ten and I go straight to bed.

Our site is under a park, in the east of the city. There is one entrance for people and one gate for the trucks. The walkway goes along the fence, and the ramp goes down into the lower area. At the moment we are working on the second platform, so the whole crew is down there and the office is almost empty.

I can read a drawing in four languages and I can operate the small machines, but I cannot drive the big one yet: I do not have the license. Last month I went to the north of England for two weeks and it rained every single day. At the weekend I am tired, so I do very little. I like the cinema, I like long walks, and I do not answer my telephone before ten in the morning.
